title: The Other Side of a Second Chance
excerpt: I spent years in prison writing plans for a life I wasn’t sure I would ever live. Now, less than a year out, I’m building Cell to Sunrise to help the next woman make her own plans real.
content:
Who would ever give me a second chance? I wasn't sure I even deserved one. Yet I still spent years in prison writing plans for a life I wasn't sure I would ever live. I wrote down goals for one year, three years, five years, and ten years. About housing, transportation, finances, family restoration, continuing education, and all the little things I knew I'd need when I came home. Still, I was terrified to walk out those gates after almost five years.

And now, less than a year out the gates, I'm looking at some of the goals I thought would take five years and realizing I'm already living them.

But I didn't get here alone. People helped me. People believed in me. People gave me opportunities when I needed them most.

Now I can't stop thinking about the women who are still sitting in prison writing their own plans, wondering if anybody will give them a chance to make those plans real, especially women without a strong support system.

I am now creating Cell to Sunrise to try to help the next woman get the opportunity to live the future she's trying to imagine.

The Future I Wrote in Prison

While I was going through some of my old prison notebooks, I almost cried.

In October 2023, I filled out a self-discovery questionnaire in my planner. One question asked what I wanted to give back to the world and how I wanted to be remembered.

I wrote that I wanted to use my talents and testimony to help others.

Then I found my reentry plans. I gave myself one year to buy a car, eighteen months to rent an apartment, and three to five years to start a business and nonprofit.

Three to five YEARS, y'all.

I haven't even been out for a year.

Yet I have a career I love, my own apartment, a car, financial stability, and a community of people who genuinely support me. I'm rebuilding my business, writing my Cell to Self, and now developing a nonprofit as we speak.

Now don't get me wrong. I haven't accomplished everything on those pages. Some of the things I want most I am still praying for and leaving in God's capable hands. My life isn't perfect, and I certainly don't have everything figured out.

But sometimes I look around in wonder as I try to keep up with all the blessings God has given me.

Because whatever God is doing in my life, it's bigger than what I planned.

I Remember What It Felt Like

When I walked out of prison in November 2025, I had a couple of outfits, hygiene supplies, a bus pass, and a whole lot of uncertainty.

I hadn't been through work release. I didn't have money saved up. I was headed to a halfway house and praying someone would give me a chance.

And those first months weren't exactly smooth sailing.

There were issues with my job, housing problems, transportation challenges, and plenty of moments when I wondered whether the stable life I'd planned in prison was ever going to happen.

Some gave me rides. Some gave me a place to stay. Some encouraged me when I needed it, and others took a chance on me professionally. Each one of those opportunities pushed me closer to my goals.

The Women I Left Behind

I still talk to over two dozen women I was incarcerated with. Women I laughed with, cried with, and prayed with. Women who held my hand while I struggled through some of the hardest moments of my life. Women who still give me hope today through their messages of encouragement and support. These women are my cheerleaders and keep me going on tough days.

Some of them have release dates coming up and absolutely no outside support. I can't just forget about where I came from because my own life is going so well.

So I'm just doing what I can. It started with random acts of kindness as I felt led, like a Lyft to work when someone was released, money for diapers, funds for commissary to get hygiene, or simply being a mentor or friend.

Sometimes it's a Walmart gift card for a woman in work release who doesn't have family. Sometimes it's buying an outfit for a woman being released directly from prison. Sometimes it's hygiene supplies, a bus pass, reconnecting family members, or researching housing programs and making phone calls.

So far, I've helped around ten women and am actively helping four more who are being released in the next 30 days.

It might not sound like a lot, but it means everything to me. And I think it means a lot to them too. Every one of those women is a real person with a story, a past, and hopefully a brighter future living in God's purpose.

Somewhere along the way, I realized how many other women are sitting in prison right now with the same fears I had. Women who want to change but don't know where to start. Women who are doing everything they can to prepare but don't have the money, connections, or support.

What if I could help more of them?

The Birth of Cell to Sunrise

I've started building a reentry planning app that I hope to one day get onto the tablets inside prisons, starting with women in Florida. It includes a vision planner and a questionnaire designed to help connect women with resources that actually fit their needs.

And these aren't just the formal, boring questions you find on government-funded assessments. They're real-life questions from someone who recently got out of a five-year bid, along with input from people who genuinely want to help.

The planning app connects to a statewide Florida resource database for women coming home from prison. Housing, transportation, employment assistance, healthcare, food resources, recovery programs, and community support. All the things that can make the difference between getting out and actually getting started.

Here's what I hope will make Cell to Sunrise different. I'm not just building another giant directory of organizations that may or may not be able to help someone. I'm researching programs across Florida to find out who they actually serve, what they require, and how women can access them. I even have volunteers willing to make phone calls when we can't get answers through email.

I want to know the details that matter when you're sitting in prison trying to figure out where you're going to go. Does this place accept women directly from prison? Can you apply before release? How much money do you need upfront? What if you're on probation?

Those are the questions that can make or break someone's reentry plan.

And I don't want Cell to Sunrise to stop at providing information. I want to continue offering practical help wherever I can, because sometimes the smallest things make the biggest difference when you're coming home.

Because finding a program online is one thing. Finding a program that will actually accept you, and having what you need when you get there, is something else entirely.

And yes, I'm still working full time, writing this blog, sponsoring women in AA, and living my own wonderfully chaotic little life.

Anyone who knows me knows I can't sit still anyway. But also, my recovery programs and the Bible tell me I can't keep what I have without giving it away.

I don't want to wait until I have some huge organization, a fancy office, or a bank account full of money to start helping people.

I can start right where I am.

Actually, I already have.

Maybe This Is What the Blessings Are For

I don't know exactly where Cell to Sunrise will go. I'm still figuring it out.

Three years ago, I wrote down the kind of difference I hoped to make in the world. I didn't know how or when I'd get there.

And now, I think I'm beginning to understand.

I keep asking God what He wants me to do with all of the blessings in my life. Because I don't believe He brought me through everything I've been through just so I could have a comfortable life and keep it all to myself.

Maybe some of the things I experienced are exactly what will allow me to reach women who might not otherwise trust someone offering help.

If you know a woman preparing to come home from prison who could use some help, or you know of a resource or organization that might make a difference, please reach out. I can't promise I can help everyone, but I can promise I'll do my best.

Welcome to Cell to Sunrise. Let's gooooo!!!!

title: You Get to Decide
excerpt: I went from fist fighting in county jail to deciding a two-hour chow line wasn't worth my sanity.
content:
Dear Prison Pals,

I am going to have to start sending y'all some of the blog posts from my other series besides the letters I write to you. I think you would really enjoy some of them. Maybe one day I'll just start copying and pasting into a message and see how many characters 20K, or whatever the limit really is!

I promised pictures, so here goes me! My room looks so simple in the picture, but in my mind, it is like a palace. Haha. And that's my little doggy, Willa. My BFF!

Actually, I think I'm going to send my latest blog at the end of this letter. It was inspired by my last letter to you when I asked if wanting a Christian man who will pray with me was too much to ask!!!

I was having a really bad day Monday. I was stuck in my head and couldn't get out. Depression and anxiety felt like they were overtaking my soul. I almost left work. I was holding back tears and screams all day.

But somewhere in the middle of all that, I had another spiritual awakening. I surrendered all the little things in my life I was still trying to control to Him. It started with a worship song in the middle of work then a prayer. Every time I think I've reached the max level of human peace, God blows my mind and shows me there's more. Crazy!

People are always asking how I seem to never let anything or anyone bother me. The truth is, I was never like that before prison. In county jail, I was a mess. Ask Tree if you don't believe me. I was getting into fist fights and being super immature.

The girl I rode with in the transport van gave me a pep talk on the way to prison, and one thing stuck with me my entire bid: "You got to decide how to do your time right now." Are you going to stress out, let every little thing bother you, and do hard time?

Now, I was still fist fighting and being a mess in reception, so apparently the wisdom didn't kick in immediately. Haha. But eventually something changed.

I looked around and saw misery, suffering, impatience, intolerance, and pain. I knew I wanted to change. I wanted to grow and get out different than I went in because the same hadn't been working for me.

I had been successful at different times in my life, but I was never truly happy. I was always anxious and running. From jobs. From myself. From God. From my family. I was high-strung, impatient, and constantly in a panic. It was no way to live.

So I set one main goal for my time in prison: balance out my mental health.

I knew God and staying clean were the top priorities. I didn't do any of it perfectly, but every time I stumbled, I got back up a little quicker and stayed up a little longer. Even through serious trauma, like my father committing suicide and then finding out truths I never thought possible, I prioritized my mental health which started with balance.

Maybe we set too many goals sometimes. We either have all this time and expect too much of ourselves, or we look at the practically nonexistent resources and expect nothing. I had plenty I wanted to accomplish, but I always circled back to my mental health. Balance became my prison mantra.

So I practiced it in the smallest, stupidest situations. The chow line, for example. If somebody skipped me, oh well. If it took two hours, they ran out of food, or we were eating at 11:45 PM, it really sucked, but I wasn't going to let it work me up. Honestly, where did I have to be that couldn't wait?

Psych was harder. I was trying to get my medication to the lowest but most effective dose while dealing with absolutely terrible prison medical care. I learned to stay calm even when I really wanted to cuss somebody out, and even when they probably deserved it. I used my manners, stood my ground, explained my goal, and kept asking them to help me accomplish it.

One of the two dozen times they randomly forgot to fill my prescription, they told me to come back in a few days. I very politely told them I would just wait right there until then. I'd worked too hard for the balance I'd achieved, so I didn't mind waiting. The nurse ended up sneaking me my meds and told me to come back at the end of pill line the next day.

Some people in there care. Most don't. But none of them were worth my sanity.

I don't even know why this is what I ended up writing to y'all about today. Maybe one of you needed to hear it. Maybe all of you did. Or maybe I'm just rambling.

Maybe your word isn't balance. Maybe it's patience. Peace. Loyalty. Faith. Discipline. Forgiveness. Hope.

Whatever it is, you don't have to become a completely different person overnight. I sure as hell didn't. I'm still trying.

But no one is worth my peace, so today I am quick to say BYEEEEEEE!

I love you guys dearly.

Love always,

I Am Amy

title: Here in the Waiting
excerpt: Today was not a good day. I looked at myself and realized I wasn't ready for the kind of relationship I'd been asking God for. Ouch.
content:
Today is not a great day.

Nothing terrible happened. No crisis. No devastating news. My life is actually really good. And yet, my head has been all over the place today, and I've wanted to burst into tears more times than I can count.

Part of it is just another fun side effect of being a woman. But part of it is anxiety. A little depression. Feeling overwhelmed. All things that rarely hit me like this anymore, but apparently today they decided to have a reunion in my head.

Normally, when I feel myself starting to spiral, I can redirect pretty quickly. Today has been harder.

The good news is that I have absolutely no desire to drink or use. Ever. God removed that desire from me completely while I was working my Steps, and I don't take that for granted. But sobriety doesn't mean my brain suddenly stopped looking for other things to obsess over.

Lately, I've been trying to realign my values with God's purpose for my life. In one of my last Dear Prison Pals posts, I asked my friends behind the gate if just wanting a strong Christian man who will pray with me was too much to ask.

And then... in walks a man from stage right, and I freeze.

I looked at myself and realized something ridiculously important that should and would probably be obvious to most normal human beings, which I am not.

I wasn't ready for the kind of relationship I'd been asking God for.

Ouch. Right?

But hear me out, because I'm not being self-deprecating. I'm not saying I'm not good enough or that I'm unworthy. I'm not saying I don't deserve a good man or that I have to become some perfectly healed, Proverbs 31 version of myself before someone can love me.

That's not what I mean at all.

I mean that I'm asking God for a spiritually mature relationship while recognizing there are places in my own spiritual life that aren't yet aligned with what I'm asking for. I don't know if I'm ready to lay out every detail of what that means yet, but there it is.

I know I talk about guys on this blog. Honestly, those are some of the funniest, rawest, most relatable moments. But if I'm really examining myself, sometimes it's an escape mechanism too.

I'm getting so close to feeling whole, but little moments like today remind me that I'm not completely there yet.

And I don't have to be. Because with little realizations like this one, I get a little bit closer to God's vision for my life.

That doesn't mean I can't be friends with someone, get to know them, laugh with them, or enjoy having them in my life. It doesn't mean a friendship couldn't eventually become something more. It just means I don't have to figure any of that out right now.

Honestly, meeting someone whose walk with God I truly admire has made me look harder at my own. Not because I want to become a better woman for someone else, but because seeing faith lived out in someone else can remind us of what we want to strengthen in ourselves.

I want to be a better human being. A better Christian whose primary purpose is to pour Jesus' love out onto other people.

And that's when I started thinking about what I've actually been asking God for.

If I expect a man's first response to be to pray with me, shouldn't prayer be my first response too?

If I expect a man to turn to biblical principles as his core values, shouldn't my values consistently reflect those same principles?

If I'm asking for someone who puts God first, shouldn't I be making sure that's exactly where I'm putting Him?

That one stung a little.

Because I truly, completely, 100% love Jesus. There is absolutely no question in my heart about that. Never has been.

But if I'm being completely honest, too often I still allow things in my life to slip in front of Him.

And that's just not okay with me.

There's so much more I can be doing. More time with God. More prayer. More Scripture. More service. More helping people. More listening and less trying to decide for myself exactly how everything is supposed to happen. Less trying to figure out who people are supposed to be in my life and more just appreciating who they are while they're there.

Less of my own writing. More of God's. God is the author. Not me.

In prison, I would listen to a song by Jamie Grace over and over again called The Waiting. I actually got overwhelmed while writing this tonight and had to stop and listen to it.

Of course I did.

A song I clung to in prison about waiting is now reminding me how to handle this exact moment in my life.

Apparently I'm still learning.

And today, while my head was spinning and I wanted to cry and obsess and crawl inside myself, I realized I had a choice about what I did next.

So I sang.

Right there in my office (granted, I was by myself), I sang my go-to worship song out loud, Lord, I Lift Your Name on High.

Then I prayed.

And when I ran out of words, I quietly spoke out loud the most powerful name in all of Heaven and Earth.

"Jesus."

Afterwards, I blasted Victory House Worship's I Want to Spend It All on You, another song that helped me survive in prison and apparently helped me survive today too.

Then tonight, I came home to hold myself accountable and write this while I'm still going through it. While I'm still emotional. While I'm still figuring out where I'm falling short and where God is asking me to grow.

While I'm still Healing in Real Time.

title: The Stuff in the Shower
excerpt: I spent years learning to keep my belongings close and always be ready to run. Then one morning, I found my shampoo sitting in the shower and realized something had changed.
content:
I don’t remember exactly when it happened. There wasn’t some huge moment where I stopped and thought, Wow. I’m free.

I just left my stuff in the bathroom.

It started with my shampoo and conditioner. I left it there in the shower and walked away.

That probably sounds completely insignificant to most people, but it wasn’t to me.

I spent over four years in prison, where you didn’t just leave your things in the shower, and if you did, you definitely didn’t assume they’d still be there when you came back. My belongings stayed with me. That’s how it worked. I carried what I needed to the shower in a contraband shower bag, used it, and carried it back to my bunk.

Then I came home from prison, but some habits took longer than others to break. But if I’m being fair, I wasn’t exactly stable before prison either. There were times when I was never 100% certain I’d be coming back to the same place each day, so I learned to keep my belongings with me. Then prison just reinforced it.

When I got out, I moved into a halfway house. The other girls picked spots in our shared bathrooms and left their toiletries there like normal people. Not me. I had a plastic tote bag at the end of my bed, and every time I went into the bathroom, it came with me. When I was done, it came right back out.

Hayley asked me about it once, and I just shook my head. No explanation.

Then I got kicked out of the halfway house, and every move I made over the next six weeks only validated the fear I’d been carrying around with that stupid little plastic bag. See? Don’t get comfortable. Always be ready to run. Homelessness, addiction, instability, and prison had all taught me that same lesson in different ways.

It’s a sad way to live, but five months out of prison, I was still living that way. I refused to own more than two duffel bags of stuff. Easier to pack up and go, just in case, I’d say. You just never know.

Then one morning, I walked into the bathroom and noticed my shampoo sitting in the shower.

Apparently, I had left it there the night before.

I just stared at it for a second and then started laughing. I had been renting a room from a great person for months. I had my own bathroom. I was safe there. Nobody was threatening to throw me out. Nobody was telling me to pack my shit. There was absolutely no logical reason I couldn’t leave a bottle of shampoo in the shower. I just couldn’t bring myself to do it.

But apparently the night before, without even realizing it, I finally had. So next I did something even crazier and I left it there.

Somewhere along the way, I had started feeling safe. Stable. Secure. I had consistency. All the things I’d craved for most of my life were creeping in so slowly and quietly that I almost didn’t notice them.

I wasn’t worried I’d come home from work and suddenly be unwelcome. I wasn’t planning where I’d go next. I wasn’t living out of a bag. Some part of me had finally started believing, I get to come back here.

Now don’t start thinking crazy like I left my toothbrush too. Baby steps, okay? That took a little longer.

Before I got out of prison, I imagined freedom in huge moments. Walking through the gate. Seeing my family. Getting a job. Driving again. Having money in my own bank account. And those things absolutely mattered.

But nobody told me that sometimes freedom would sneak up on me in a bathroom. Nobody told me about the moments when my brain would suddenly realize, Oh. We don’t have to do that anymore.

Once I noticed it, I started seeing those moments everywhere. I could decide when to shower. I could choose what shampoo I wanted. I could close the bathroom door and be alone. I could buy something without worrying about whether it was sold on commissary and would get taken. LOL.

I didn’t have to carry everything with me anymore. I didn’t have to be ready to run.

Freedom doesn’t always arrive looking like freedom. Sometimes it looks so ordinary I almost miss it. Like this post on Facebook from a few days ago:

Today, I have my own apartment, and y’all, I have way more than two duffel bags. I have a bathroom absolutely full of my stuff. My shampoo stays in my shower, and my toothbrush stays by my sink.

Some days I still wake up and think someone is going to tap me on the shoulder and say, “I’m sorry, ma’am. This actually isn’t your life. We gave you the wrong one and have to ask you to return it.”

But I’m getting there.

I spent so much of my life being ready to run that I didn’t know how to recognize the moment I finally felt safe enough to stop.

I guess sometimes God’s biggest blessings show up in the most ordinary places. Sometimes freedom simply feels like leaving my shampoo in the shower and walking away.
